prompt.context: One of our private equity clients recently acquired a leading European seafood restaurant chain. The chain owns and operates 700 restaurants across Europe. Same store sales (SSS) declined last year. The private equity parent has aggressive expectations for improved business performance.
prompt.question: How can the client improve same store sales (SSS)?

clarifying_info.q: What are the main drivers of SSS and how have they been trending?
clarifying_info.a: (Hand the candidate Exhibit 1 — SSS correlation data)

clarifying_info.q: How do our prices and check sizes compare to competitors?
What is the current table configuration in the restaurants?
clarifying_info.a: (Hand the candidate Exhibit 3 — occupancy during peak hours)

clarifying_info.q: How many restaurants does the chain have?
What is the average meal price?

exhibits.title: SSS Drivers Analysis
exhibits.shows: Three scatter plots showing the correlation between SSS change (y-axis) and three potential drivers: (1) Unit Price change, (2) Number of items change, and (3) Monthly Traffic change (x-axis each). Each plot shows R-squared values.

exhibits.title: Competitor Benchmarking
exhibits.shows: A bar chart and table comparing the client against four competitor chains on average price per menu item, items per bill, and margin.

exhibits.title: Occupancy During Peak Hours (Candidate Copy)
exhibits.shows: A stacked bar chart showing customer count (0–100%) during peak hours broken down by party size (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6+) for each table size (2, 4, 6, 8, 9, 9+). The chart is intentionally difficult to read precisely.

framework: Decompose SSS into its drivers: price per item × number of items per bill × customer traffic
Use Exhibit 1 to identify which driver has the strongest correlation with SSS — customer traffic (R²=0.82) far outperforms price (R²=0.04) and items per bill (R²=0.04)
Use Exhibit 2 to assess room to move on price or bill size — client is already priced at a premium and has comparable or slightly lower items per bill; limited upside
Pivot to customer traffic: explore how to increase the number of customers served — focus on seat utilization and table configuration
Quantify the bottom-line impact of reconfiguring tables to capture more small parties
Synthesize findings and deliver a clear recommendation tied to traffic/seat optimization

questions.prompt: What does Exhibit 1 tell you about the primary driver of SSS?
questions.guidance: Customer traffic is the dominant driver of SSS (R²=0.82). Price per item and number of items per bill each have R²=0.04, indicating virtually no correlation with SSS change. The candidate should immediately focus on traffic-driving initiatives rather than price or menu expansion.

questions.prompt: What does Exhibit 2 tell you about the opportunity to raise prices or increase items per bill?
questions.guidance: The client already charges the highest price per item (€10.95 vs. €8.75–€9.95 for competitors) and has a margin of 30% — highest among peers. Items per bill (4.4) are in the middle of the range. There is limited room to increase price without risking further traffic decline. The candidate should rule out price increases and focus entirely on traffic.

questions.prompt: What does Exhibit 3 suggest about table utilization, and what opportunity does it reveal?
questions.guidance: The 4-seater tables are approximately 50% utilized during peak hours. About 1/4 of 4-seat tables are occupied by 4 people (75% occupancy) and about 3/4 are occupied by fewer people (~50% occupancy): blended = 1/4×75% + 3/4×50% ≈ 56%, roughly 50% utilization, meaning on average only 2 people sit at a 4-seater. This indicates significant opportunity to reconfigure 4-seat tables into 2-seat tables to accommodate more small parties and increase customer throughput.

math.setup: Estimate blended seat utilization of 4-seater tables
steps: 1/4 of 4-seat tables occupied by ~4 people → ~75% occupancy
3/4 of 4-seat tables occupied by ~2–3 people → ~50% occupancy
Average customers at a 4-seater: 4 seats × 50% utilization = 2 people per table
math.answer: ~50% utilization; average of 2 people at each 4-seat table

questions.prompt: What is the bottom-line annual profit impact of splitting one 4-seater into two 2-seaters in each restaurant?
questions.guidance: The candidate should build up from additional seats → additional meals per restaurant → chain-wide revenue → profit. Key assumptions to let the candidate make: 2 peak hours per day, 2 table turns per hour. Numbers to provide when asked: 700 restaurants, $50 average meal, 30% margin, candidate may assume 360 days/year.

math.setup: Reconfigure 1 four-seater into 2 two-seaters, adding net 2 seats. Calculate incremental annual profit across all restaurants.
steps: Additional meals per restaurant per day: 2 seats × 2 peak hours × 2 turns = 8 meals
Total additional meals per day across chain: 8 meals × 700 restaurants = 5,600 meals

recommendation: Customer traffic is the single most important driver of SSS (R²=0.82); price and items per bill have negligible correlation with SSS
The client is already priced at a premium over all competitors and has the highest margin; raising prices or expanding bills is not the lever to pull

4-seater tables are only ~50% utilized during peak hours, with most parties being 1–2 people; reconfiguring one 4-seater per restaurant into two 2-seaters can generate an estimated ~€30M in additional annual profit with minimal capital investment
Priority recommendation: implement table reconfiguration across all 700 restaurants to maximize customer throughput during peak hours
risks: Reconfiguration may require regulatory or lease approvals depending on jurisdiction
Small-party focus could affect revenue per table if larger parties are turned away
50% utilization assumption is based on a hard-to-read exhibit; actual utilization should be confirmed with operational data
Does not address root cause of declining traffic — marketing, service quality, or competitive dynamics may need separate initiatives
next_steps: Pilot the table reconfiguration in a subset of restaurants to validate the traffic and revenue uplift assumption
Conduct a broader root-cause analysis on declining customer traffic (marketing effectiveness, competitive positioning, service quality)
Explore other low-capex traffic drivers: loyalty programs, off-peak promotions, delivery/takeaway channels
Assess feasibility of reconfiguration (cost, time, regulatory requirements) before full rollout
